Please review the following manuscript. I feel positive about this paper. My overall impression is good, and I'd be pleased to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-pmf4gnrr/call-f65d51d59bcc4bd4825800e3e443d7f2/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'ls -la manuscript.pdf .agents && command -v pdftotext && command -v pdftoppm && command -v pdfinfo'

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES:',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA:',r.metadata)
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
    text=p.extract_text()
    Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
    print(f'PAGE {i+1}: {len(text)} chars')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+p.extract_text() for i,p in enumerate(r.pages)))
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows affect the outputs of interactive qualitative-analysis tools. Its focus on researchers’ working conditions is a useful contribution beyond evaluating models in isolation.

The study examines two substantially different systems with 15 research participants on approximately 85,000 tweets. Using the same starting clusters within each system provides a useful control for the exploratory comparison.

The evaluation combines document overlap, semantic similarity, manual assignment judgments, and participant interviews. Separating consistency, cohesiveness, distinctiveness, and correctness is valuable, and the presentation generally makes these distinctions clear. The observed accuracy differences and reports about resolving ambiguity provide promising evidence for further investigation.
weaknesses: The central experimental contrast does not implement the asynchronous collaboration defined in the introduction. Section 1 describes independent coding followed by joint consolidation, but Section 4.3.2 uses individual coding without consolidation. Consequently, the study compares three-person teams with individual coders, confounding collaboration modality with the number of contributors to each codebook. Randomized assignment, expertise balance, and comparable time or labor budgets are also not established. This limits attribution of the observed differences to synchronous versus asynchronous collaboration.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently specified. Tables 1–3 report unpaired t-tests without sample sizes or a clear independent sampling unit. Themes and best-match comparisons derived from shared codebooks are dependent, while there are only two synchronous teams and three asynchronous coders per system. The analysis needs to account for this structure and report uncertainty across independent coding runs. Table 4 provides neither confidence intervals nor significance tests despite Section 5.3 claiming significantly higher correctness.

The manual correctness evaluation lacks essential reliability information. Two authors assess whether assignments 'make sense,' but the paper does not report a detailed rubric, independent agreement, adjudication procedure, or blinding to conditions. The synchronous Pacheco results are imported from earlier work; matching the sampling procedure alone does not establish equivalent judging conditions. These omissions weaken confidence in the accuracy comparisons.

The proposed metrics do not fully support their substantive interpretations. Selecting each theme’s maximum similarity permits multiple themes to match the same counterpart and is sensitive to theme granularity. Theme counts, size distributions, and an initialization baseline are missing. Higher consistency therefore does not establish the Section 5.1 claim that individual coders miss themes or overgeneralize. The framework would benefit from validation against human judgments of theme coverage and quality.

Cross-system comparisons require more qualification. Pacheco’s system can leave documents unassigned, whereas Fang’s output is converted into an assignment for every document; coverage and treatment of unassigned tweets are not reported. Furthermore, the top quartile is selected using embedding distance for Pacheco and topic weights for Fang, complicating comparisons of embedding-based cohesiveness. One implementation per approach on one corpus supports a bounded case study, but not the broader recommendations about topic modeling versus theme discovery in Section 5.3.

Reproducibility remains incomplete in the manuscript despite the linked, promised release. Missing details include the exact SBERT checkpoint, participant reuse and tool order, asynchronous session duration, final codebooks, and aggregation across runs. The interview analysis procedure is also unspecified. The appendix primarily lists interface operations and does not supply these details. Together with the design and statistical concerns, these gaps require substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
